opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic picture is that we've been on a really steep compute trend, something like four to five x per year in the compute used for frontier training runs, and that's been driven by a mix of things: more money being spent, hardware getting better per dollar, and labs getting better at actually using big clusters efficiently. The question is how long that can continue.

My rough expectation is that the trend continues at something like its current pace for the next few years, maybe through 2028 or so. There's a lot of investment already committed. The big labs and hyperscalers are building multi-gigawatt data centers, and the capex numbers are enormous. So the next couple of generations of training runs are already partially baked in.

Then somewhere in the late 2020s to early 2030s you start running into real constraints. One is just money. If you extrapolate, you get to training runs that cost tens of billions and then hundreds of billions of dollars, and at that point you need the AI revenue to justify it, or you need investors who believe very strongly in the trajectory. Another is power. Getting many gigawatts of power to a single site, or a set of coordinated sites, is a serious bottleneck, because grid buildout and permitting are slow. And then there's chip production: fab capacity at TSMC, advanced packaging, high-bandwidth memory. Those supply chains can expand, but not instantly.

So my median is that by around 2030 the scaling slows down. Maybe it goes from 4–5x per year toward something more like 2x per year, driven mostly by hardware efficiency improvements and slower growth in spending. That slowdown matters a lot for forecasting. If we haven't hit something like fully automated AI R&D by the time scaling slows, then timelines get substantially longer, because you lose one of the main drivers of progress. Algorithmic progress continues, but algorithmic progress itself partly depends on having lots of compute for experiments.

The big caveat is that it could go the other way. If AI systems start generating a lot of economic value, say automating large chunks of software engineering, then the revenue could justify much more spending, and you could see even faster scaling. You could even see something like a national-project level of investment. So I'd say there's a fairly bimodal flavor to it: either AI gets very powerful relatively soon, around the time compute is still scaling fast, or progress slows noticeably in the early 2030s and things take longer. I put a fair amount of weight on both scenarios, which is part of why I think the next few years are especially important.

r002.rationale: It predicts scaling will slow around 2030 due to investment, chip-production, and power constraints, and describes slower progress in the early 2030s if very powerful AI has not arrived sooner.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the right way to think about this is that there are basically a few different inputs that have been driving the increase in compute used for frontier training runs, and most of them are going to slow down sometime around the early 2030s.

So historically, training compute for the largest runs has been going up something like four to five x per year. And that's coming from a few things stacked on top of each other. One is just hardware getting better per dollar, which is maybe 1.3 to 1.5x per year or so. And then the much bigger factor is just spending more money. Companies have been scaling investment extremely fast, going from spending tens of millions on a training run to hundreds of millions to billions, and now people are talking about hundred billion dollar clusters.

The thing is, that spending growth can't continue indefinitely. At some point you're talking about a meaningful fraction of global GDP, you're talking about the total amount of chip fabrication capacity that exists, the power that exists. So my expectation is that through maybe 2028 or 2030, you continue to see really fast scaling, roughly on the current trend, maybe slightly slower. And then after that, if AI hasn't already become transformative enough to be dramatically accelerating the economy, you'd expect the growth in compute to slow down to something closer to the underlying hardware improvement rate plus some modest increase in investment. So maybe you go from 4x a year to more like 2x a year, or something in that range.

But I think there's a really important caveat here, which is that this is conditional on AI not being super transformative by then. If we end up with systems that can substantially automate AI research, or more broadly automate a lot of cognitive labor, then the picture changes a lot. You could see much higher willingness to invest, because the returns are obviously enormous, and you could also see AI accelerating the hardware side, chip design, fab construction, all of that. So in some sense the compute trajectory and the capabilities trajectory are pretty entangled.

The other thing I'd flag is that training compute isn't the only story anymore. There's been a lot of movement toward inference-time compute, RL, these approaches where you're spending a lot of compute running the models rather than just training them. And that changes how you'd want to think about scaling, because the question is less "how big is the biggest training run" and more "how much total compute is going into making these systems better and deploying them," which could continue to scale even if individual pretraining runs plateau.

So I guess the summary would be: continued fast scaling for the next few years, probably some slowdown around the early 2030s driven by economic and physical constraints, unless AI capabilities are dramatic enough by then to change the economics, in which case all bets are off and things could get quite wild.

r002.rationale: The candidate predicts compute growth will slow around the early 2030s due to investment and physical constraints, conditional on AI not becoming transformative by then.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between how much compute we could physically build and how much people will actually be willing to pay for. Through the early 2030s, I think there’s room for substantial growth, but I wouldn’t just extrapolate the recent rate indefinitely.

You can spend more money, manufacture more chips, and get more computation out of each chip. But as you get to very large investments, power and construction become substantial constraints, and the economic case matters a lot more. If AI systems are generating enormous revenues, or doing useful AI research, then spending much more could make sense. If capabilities or revenues disappoint, scaling could slow down considerably.

There’s also a distinction between physical compute and what you can accomplish with it. Improvements in algorithms could let you get substantially more capability from the same hardware. And compute can go toward training a larger model or toward having existing models spend more time solving problems. So even a slowdown in the growth of training runs wouldn’t necessarily imply a comparable slowdown in capabilities.

My basic expectation is continued substantial scaling, with increasing uncertainty about the pace as we approach the early 2030s. A particularly important uncertainty is whether AI starts materially accelerating the research that makes further progress possible.

r001.rationale: The response discusses substantial compute growth but does not mention scaling training compute to roughly 10^30 FLOP by 2030 or say that this would sustain previously observed progress trends.

r002.rationale: It says scaling could slow if capabilities or revenues disappoint and notes power, construction, and economic constraints. It does not clearly make that prediction conditional on very powerful AI not yet being achieved in the early 2030s.

sol-6.1.text:
I expect the amount of compute used for the largest training runs to keep increasing pretty rapidly for at least the next few years. But I’d distinguish between how much money people spend, how much compute they get per dollar, and how effectively they use that compute. Those can all improve, and they have different constraints.

The spending component eventually gets difficult to sustain. You can go from a billion-dollar training run to a ten-billion-dollar training run, but you can’t keep multiplying spending indefinitely. By the early 2030s, continued growth at recent rates would require a pretty substantial fraction of investment in the economy. Whether that happens depends a lot on whether AI is generating enough revenue and looks sufficiently valuable to justify it.

Power and chip production are also constraints, though I wouldn’t treat either as a fixed ceiling. If there’s enough demand and enough lead time, people can build more infrastructure. The question is how quickly.

So my expectation is continued substantial scaling, with more uncertainty about the rate as we get into the early 2030s. And that doesn’t directly tell you how quickly capabilities improve: algorithmic progress and spending more compute at inference could matter a lot, even if the growth in training compute slows.
